description.summary: The Haetae (also Haechi) is a legendary guardian beast from Korean and Chinese mythology, depicted as a muscular lion-like creature with scales and a single horn, revered as a symbol of justice, law, and protection against fire.
description.full: The Haetae (Korean: 해태; Hanja: 獬豸), known in Chinese as Xiezhi (xièzhì), is a mythological creature shared across East Asian traditions that has taken on particular cultural importance in Korea. In Korean tradition the creature is described as having a muscular leonine body covered with sharp scales, a bell at its neck, and a single long horn on its forehead. The creature is believed to possess great intellect and the innate ability to distinguish right from wrong; according to legend, it would ram the guilty with its horn while sparing the innocent. This judicial quality made the haetae an enduring symbol of law and justice across the region. Stone statues of the haetae guard the gates of Gyeongbokgung Palace in Seoul, where they were placed during the Joseon dynasty to ward off fire disasters. In China, law enforcement officials wore xiezhi crowns from the Qin and Han dynasties onward, and Tang-dynasty censors wore xiezhi hats during impeachment proceedings. The creature continues in modern use: the Haechi cartoon character serves as the official mascot of Seoul, and the People's Republic of China engraves xiezhi imagery on court gavels. In 2022, the prehistoric giraffoid species Discokeryx xiezhi was scientifically named in reference to the creature's distinctive horn.

etymology.origin: The Korean name 해태 (haetae) is a Korean reading of the Chinese characters 獬豸. Linguist Axel Schuessler reconstructs the Late Han pronunciation as *gɛʔ-ḍɛʔ* and proposes an Austroasiatic etymology related to words for deer or stag in Old Mon, Old Khmer, and Burmese.
etymology.meaning: The characters 獬豸 refer to a mythical beast that distinguishes guilt from innocence. The English descriptive name 'unicorn-lion' references its single horn and leonine body.
etymology.first_use: Earliest literary mentions appear in Han dynasty texts: Sima Xiangru's 'Rhapsody on the Imperial Park' and Wang Chong's Lunheng (c. 80 CE).

origins.cultural_roots: The xiezhi/haetae originates in ancient Chinese mythology and was employed in judicial ritual from at least the Han dynasty. It was adopted into Korean court culture during the Joseon dynasty and integrated into palace architecture as a fire-protective guardian.
origins.earliest_accounts: Wang Chong's Lunheng (c. 80 CE) documents the judicial application; Sima Xiangru's Han-dynasty rhapsody contains earlier references. Korean adoption is associated with the Joseon dynasty (1392–1897).
origins.folklore_connections: Part of a broader East Asian tradition of guardian beasts at architectural thresholds, related to Chinese guardian lions (shishi) and the auspicious qilin.

history.modern_era: The haetae remains an active symbol in Korean civic life: haetae statues are a defining visual element of Gyeongbokgung Palace, and the Seoul city government uses the cartoon Haechi character as its official mascot. The Republic of China military police wear xiezhi badge insignia, and PRC law courts engrave the creature on gavels.

physical.name: Gyeongbokgung Palace haetae statues
physical.description: Stone statues of the haetae positioned at the gates of Gyeongbok Palace in Seoul, placed during the Joseon dynasty to ward off fire disasters.
physical.analysis: Physical artifacts in situ at a major UNESCO-recognized heritage site. Document the institutional role of the haetae as protective symbol in Korean court culture.

documentary.name: Lunheng by Wang Chong (c. 80 CE)
documentary.description: Han dynasty philosophical text documenting the judicial application of the xiezhi in criminal proceedings under Emperor Shun.
documentary.analysis: Earliest clearly dated written account of the creature's judicial role.

scientific.name: Austroasiatic linguistic origin
scientific.description: Linguist Axel Schuessler proposes the Chinese name 獬豸 derives from an Austroasiatic root related to words for 'deer' or 'stag' in Old Mon, Old Khmer, and Burmese, suggesting the myth may have originated with accounts of actual horned animals.
evidence_cited: Comparative linguistics analysis of Late Han pronunciation reconstruction

skeptical.name: Judicial-political allegory
skeptical.description: The haetae/xiezhi is best understood as a symbolic construct designed to legitimate judicial authority and reinforce norms of official accountability, rather than a belief in a literal animal.
proponents: General scholarly consensus in folklore and legal history
evidence_cited: Consistent depiction on judicial insignia across multiple dynasties
Absence of any eyewitness encounter tradition

folklore.beliefs: In Korean tradition, haetae statues at palace and temple gates actively protect the buildings from fire and evil. The creature's presence is apotropaic rather than merely decorative.
